title: The Bipolar Transistor Amplifier: Small-Signal Analysis & Frequency Response

content.aim: To study small-signal operation of a bipolar transistor amplifier and to measure its voltage gain, phase shift and frequency response. The experiment covers common-emitter and common-collector (emitter follower) configurations, including effect of emitter bypass capacitor on gain and bandwidth.
objectives: To understand small-signal operation when small AC signal is superimposed on DC bias in active region.
To construct and test common-emitter amplifier with voltage-divider bias, coupling capacitors and emitter bypass capacitor.
To construct and test common-collector (emitter follower) amplifier and verify unity gain, zero phase shift, high input impedance and low output impedance.
To measure voltage gain Av, current gain Ai, input resistance Rin and output resistance Rout.
To observe 180° phase inversion in CE and 0° phase in emitter follower on dual-trace oscilloscope.
To sweep frequency from 10Hz to 1MHz, plot Bode gain plot and determine lower cutoff fL, upper cutoff fH and bandwidth.

theory.text:
Small-Signal Amplification Principle

A transistor amplifier operates on superposition: small AC signal vin(t) is superimposed on DC quiescent bias. When biased in active region, transconductance converts small base-emitter voltage variations into collector current variations:

\[\mathit{i}_{c}(t) = \mathit{g}_{m} \mathit{v}_{be}(t) = \beta \mathit{i}_{b}(t)\]

where gm = IC/VT ≈ IC/26mV at room temperature, VT = kT/q ≈25.86mV.

Dynamic emitter resistance:

\[\mathit{r}_{e} = \mathit{V}_{T}/\mathit{I}_{E} \approx 26mV/\mathit{I}_{E}(mA)\]

For IE ≈5.25mA, re ≈26/5.25 = 4.95Ω.

Common-Emitter Gain

Case 1: Emitter resistor unbypassed (CE disconnected)

AC signal sees re + RE in emitter, output taken at collector vout = -ic RC. Negative sign indicates increased vin raises ic, increasing drop across RC and lowering collector voltage:

\[\mathit{A}_{v} = -\mathit{R}_{C}/(\mathit{r}_{e}+\mathit{R}_{E})\]

Since re << RE, Av ≈ -RC/RE = -1000/100 = -10.0 (20dB). Measured value about 9.5, close to theory.

Case 2: Emitter resistor bypassed with CE = 100µF

At midband, XCE = 1/(2πfCE) is small (1.59Ω at 1kHz) compared to RE, so RE is AC shorted. Emitter is AC ground:

\[\mathit{A}_{v} = -\mathit{R}_{C}/\mathit{r}_{e} \approx -1000/4.95 = -202\]

In practice, with source resistance and finite ro ≈20kΩ, loaded gain is 80-120 (38-42dB) with 180° inversion. Measured gain about 85 (38.59dB).

Emitter Follower (Common-Collector)

Collector tied to VCC (AC ground), input to base, output from emitter across RE:

\[\mathit{A}_{v} = \mathit{R}_{E}/(\mathit{r}_{e}+\mathit{R}_{E}) \approx 100/104.95 = 0.953 ≈1.0\]

\[\mathit{R}_{in} = \mathit{R}_{B1}||\mathit{R}_{B2}||[(\beta+1)(\mathit{r}_{e}+\mathit{R}_{E})] \approx 7.1k\Omega\]

\[\mathit{R}_{out} = \mathit{R}_{E}||(\mathit{r}_{e}+(\mathit{R}_{s}||\mathit{R}_{TH})/(\beta+1)) \approx 7.6\Omega\]

Follower has near-unity gain, 0° phase, moderately high input resistance and very low output resistance (<10Ω), suitable as buffer.

Frequency Response Analysis

Gain varies with frequency in three regions:

• Low-frequency (f < fL): Gain falls at 20dB/decade per pole due to coupling capacitors Cin, Cout and bypass CE. Dominant pole is usually due to CE because it sees low resistance (RE || [re + RTH/(β+1)]). Lower cutoff fL is approximately highest of individual pole frequencies. In this experiment, fL≈100Hz, higher than calculated 33.5Hz for CE alone because Cin and Cout also contribute.

• Midband (fL ≤ f ≤ fH): Capacitors act as shorts, internal transistor capacitances as opens. Gain flat, phase -180° for CE.

• High-frequency (f > fH): Gain rolls off due to internal capacitances Cπ≈25pF and Cμ≈8pF. Miller effect multiplies Cμ: Cin(Miller)=Cμ(1+Av)=8pF*(86)≈688pF. This large capacitance shunts base signal to ground, setting upper cutoff fH≈450kHz. At 1MHz, gain dropped to 33 and phase reached -250° due to additional poles.

Gain-bandwidth product GBW = Av0 * fH ≈85*450kHz=38.25MHz, below ft≈250-300MHz of 2N2222, as expected because ft is measured with collector shorted and represents frequency where current gain falls to unity.

Emitter follower has wider bandwidth than CE because it has no Miller multiplication (Av≈1, so Miller effect negligible). Its high-frequency cutoff is primarily due to Cπ and source resistance.

Additional Analysis: Input and Output Resistance Measurement

Input resistance Rin can be measured by inserting known series resistor Rs in input path and measuring voltage division: Vin' = Vgen * Rin/(Rs+Rin). Alternatively, Rin = RB1||RB2||rπ for CE with unbypassed RE, or RB1||RB2||[(β+1)(re+RE)] with RE. In this experiment, unbypassed Rin≈11.2kΩ, bypassed Rin≈1.45kΩ, showing bypass capacitor reduces input resistance because emitter sees only re instead of re+RE, reducing impedance looking into base. Emitter follower Rin≈7.1kΩ, higher than bypassed CE but lower than unbypassed CE.

Output resistance Rout for CE is approximately RC (1kΩ) because collector sees high impedance looking into transistor (ro≈20kΩ) in parallel with RC, so Rout≈RC||ro≈0.95kΩ≈1kΩ. For emitter follower, Rout = RE || [re + (Rs||RTH)/(β+1)] ≈7.6Ω, very low, allowing driving low-impedance loads like 8Ω speaker or 50Ω cable without significant voltage division. This was verified by loading follower with 100Ω resistor and observing small drop in output amplitude, whereas CE output dropped significantly with same load.

Gain-Bandwidth Product and Miller Effect

Gain-bandwidth product GBW = Av0 * fH is approximately constant for given bias and transistor. For CE with bypassed RE, Av0=85, fH=450kHz, GBW=38.25MHz. This is below transition frequency fT≈250-300MHz of 2N2222, which is frequency where current gain falls to unity with collector shorted. GBW < fT because voltage gain involves RC and not just current gain.

Miller effect is significant in inverting amplifiers like CE. Feedback capacitance Cμ (collector-base junction capacitance) between input and output is multiplied by (1+Av) when viewed from input, giving Cin(Miller)=Cμ(1+Av). For Av=85, Cμ=8pF, Cin(Miller)=688pF, which dominates high-frequency response. This capacitance forms low-pass filter with source resistance, causing gain to roll off at 20dB/decade above fH. To mitigate Miller effect, cascode configuration (CE followed by CB) is used, where CB stage presents low input impedance to CE collector, reducing voltage gain of CE stage and thus Miller multiplication, extending bandwidth. This is common in wideband amplifiers and op-amp input stages.

Low-Frequency Response and Coupling Capacitors

Low-frequency cutoff is set by coupling capacitors Cin, Cout and bypass capacitor CE. Each capacitor sees resistance: Cin sees Rs + Rin, Cout sees RC + RL, CE sees RE || [re + (Rs||RTH)/(β+1)]. Pole frequencies fL = 1/(2πRC). Overall fL is approximately highest of individual poles because -3dB frequency dominated by largest pole. In this experiment, CE pole calculated as 33.5Hz, but measured fL=100Hz, indicating Cin or Cout poles also contribute and are higher than CE pole. Using larger capacitors would lower fL, extending low-frequency response, at cost of larger physical size and cost.

Bode Plot Construction

Bode gain plot uses logarithmic frequency axis and linear gain in dB. Midband gain flat, low-frequency roll-off +20dB/decade per pole, high-frequency roll-off -20dB/decade per pole. Phase plot shows -45° per pole at cutoff, approaching -90° per pole far from cutoff. For CE with 180° inversion, low-frequency phase approaches -90° (due to high-pass) and high-frequency phase approaches -270° (due to low-pass plus inversion). Measured phase at 10Hz -105°, at 100Hz -160°, at 1kHz -180°, at 100kHz -188°, at 1MHz -250°, consistent with multiple poles.

procedure: TPS-3371 trainer was connected to power supply and 2N2222 transistor inserted. Voltage-divider bias network RB1=91kΩ, RB2=15kΩ, RC=1.0kΩ, RE=100Ω was wired and +12V applied. DC voltages VB, VC, VE were measured to confirm active bias with VCE>1V and VBE≈0.7V, giving IC≈5.25mA as in Table 302.1.

Coupling capacitors Cin=10µF at base and Cout=10µF at collector were connected. Audio signal generator set to 1kHz sine wave with amplitude 50mVp-p. Oscilloscope Channel 1 connected across input after Cin and Channel 2 across output after Cout, both on AC coupling. Common ground ensured for generator, scope and trainer to avoid hum and ground loop interference.

With CE disconnected (unbypassed), output voltage Vout measured and voltage gain Av=Vout/Vin calculated. Gain about 9.5 (19.55dB) with 180° phase inversion observed on dual-trace display. Inversion occurs because increased base voltage raises IC, increasing drop across RC and lowering collector voltage.

100µF electrolytic capacitor CE connected across RE with correct polarity (positive to emitter, negative to ground). Output amplitude increased sharply from ~0.5V to ~4.25V. Input kept at 50mVp-p to avoid clipping. Bypassed gain measured as Av≈85 (38.59dB) with 180° inversion, as listed in Table 302.2.

Frequency response measured by keeping input constant at 50mVp-p and varying frequency from 10Hz to 1MHz as listed in Table 302.2. At each frequency, Vout and phase shift recorded, Av and gain in dB (20log10 Av) computed. Lower -3dB frequency fL where gain falls to 0.707 of midband and upper -3dB frequency fH similarly identified. Bandwidth BW = fH - fL calculated as 449.9kHz.

Circuit rewired to common-collector (emitter follower) as per Schematic 3: collector to +12V, input to base via Cin, output from emitter across RE via Cout. Gain and phase measured, confirming Av≈0.96 and 0° phase shift. Low output impedance verified by loading test.
precautions: Input AC amplitude kept small (10-15mV peak at base) to maintain linear operation and avoid harmonic distortion and clipping that occurs when exponential diode characteristic is driven with large signal.
Electrolytic capacitor polarity checked before connection. Reverse connection causes high leakage, heating and bias distortion.
Common ground maintained for oscilloscope probes, signal generator and DC supply to avoid ground loop interference and 50Hz hum that can obscure small signals.

Oscilloscope input coupling set to AC when observing small AC signals superimposed on large DC levels at collector to keep trace on screen, and 10X probe used to reduce capacitive loading at high frequencies.
content.discussion:
Common-emitter amplifier results show classic trade-off between gain, linearity and bandwidth.

Unbypassed (CE disconnected): Gain Av≈-RC/(re+RE)≈-9.5 (19.55dB). RE provides negative feedback, stabilizing gain against hFE variation, increasing input resistance to about 11.2kΩ and widening bandwidth. This configuration is more linear and stable.

Bypassed (CE=100µF): RE is AC shorted, leaving only re=4.95Ω in emitter. Gain increases to Av≈85 (38.59dB). The increase was clearly observed when CE was connected. Higher gain comes with lower input impedance (~1.45kΩ) and greater sensitivity to overdrive, with output clipping if input too large. Measured gain of 85 is lower than theoretical -202 due to source resistance, finite transistor output resistance ro≈20kΩ and loading.

Phase relationship: CE output showed 180° inversion. When input swings positive, VBE increases, IB and IC increase, voltage drop across RC increases, so VC = VCC - IC RC decreases. Hence positive input produces negative output. This was verified on dual-trace oscilloscope with CH2 inverted relative to CH1.

Frequency Response (Graph 302.1):

• Low-frequency roll-off: Below 100Hz, gain decreased. At 100Hz, XCE = 1/(2π*100*100µF) = 15.9Ω, no longer negligible compared to re, so feedback reappears. Coupling capacitors Cin and Cout also contribute high-pass filtering. Measured fL=100Hz where gain dropped to 60 (35.56dB, -3dB from midband 85).

• Midband (200Hz-100kHz): Gain remained flat within ±0.5dB around 38.5dB, phase constant at -180°. External capacitors act as shorts, internal capacitances as opens, as expected.

• High-frequency roll-off: Above 100kHz, gain fell due to internal Cbe and Cbc. Miller multiplication of Cbc gives Cin(Miller)≈688pF, which shunts base signal to ground, creating low-pass pole at fH≈450kHz where gain again fell to 60. At 1MHz, gain dropped to 33 and phase reached -250° due to additional poles. Gain-bandwidth product GBW=Av0*fH=85*450kHz=38.25MHz, below ft of 2N2222 (250-300MHz).

Emitter Follower:

Gain measured as 0.96 (-0.35dB) with 0° phase, confirming buffer action. Input resistance ~7.1kΩ and output resistance ~7.8Ω consistent with theory. Low output resistance allows driving low-impedance loads without significant attenuation, unlike CE stage with Rout≈RC=1kΩ. This is why follower is used as output stage to drive cables, headphones and speakers.

Overall, small-signal models, including Miller effect, were validated by measured frequency response. The experiment shows why CE is used for voltage gain and CC as impedance buffer in multistage amplifiers, and why bypass capacitor is standard technique to increase AC gain without affecting DC bias.

content.conclusion:
Common-emitter amplifier provided voltage gain of 38.59dB (Av=85) with 180° phase inversion. Effect of emitter bypass capacitor in increasing AC gain from about 10 to 85 was confirmed. Bode plot showed bandwidth of 449.9kHz from fL=100Hz to fH=450kHz. Emitter follower exhibited near-unity gain (0.96), 0° phase and low output impedance of 7.8Ω, confirming suitability as buffer for impedance matching. Experiment linked small-signal theory, including Miller effect and frequency response analysis, to measured results.

questions.question: What are the main differences in a circuit using an NPN from that of a PNP transistor?
questions.answer: NPN requires positive VCC relative to emitter, base biased about +0.7V above emitter, current enters collector and base and exits emitter, majority carriers electrons in emitter/collector with higher mobility (µn≈1350 cm²/Vs) giving higher ft. PNP requires negative supply or positive emitter rail, base biased -0.7V relative to emitter, current enters emitter and exits base/collector, majority carriers holes (µp≈480 cm²/Vs) giving lower ft. Electrolytic capacitor polarities reversed: for NPN positive faces base/collector (higher DC), for PNP positive faces ground or external circuit.

questions.question: List five distinct industrial and practical applications of Bi-polar Transistor Amplifiers.
questions.answer:
• Audio preamplifier stages for microphones and sensors to amplify microvolt signals with low noise.
• RF and IF amplifiers in radio receivers and transceivers to amplify high-frequency carriers before detection.
• Active filters and equalizers using RC networks with BJT gain to realize low-pass, high-pass and band-pass responses with controllable Q.
• Impedance buffers and line drivers: emitter follower as output stage to drive cables, headphones and low-impedance loads without loading.
• Sensor signal conditioning and instrumentation: differential BJT pairs form input stages of op-amps and biomedical instruments like ECG/EEG.

questions.question: What are your physical observations and analytical deductions when the input signal frequency is varied from very low to very high frequencies?
questions.answer:
Low frequency (10-100Hz): Output amplitude decreased as frequency decreased. Capacitive reactance XC=1/(2πfC) increases, coupling capacitors form high-pass dividers and CE fails to short RE, introducing feedback that reduces gain. Phase deviates from -180° due to capacitor phase shift.
Midband (200Hz-100kHz): Output constant at 4.25Vp-p (Av=85) with 180° inversion. External capacitors act as shorts, internal capacitances as opens.
High frequency (>100kHz): Output attenuated rapidly with extra phase lag beyond 180° (up to -250° at 1MHz). Internal depletion and diffusion capacitances Cbe and Cbc cause this. Miller effect reflects Cbc to input as large shunt capacitance, bypassing high-frequency input to ground, forming low-pass pole.

questions.question: What is the phase shift between the input and output signals in a Common Emitter amplifier versus an Emitter Follower amplifier? Explain the physical mechanism.
questions.answer:
Common-emitter: 180° inversion. Positive input increases VBE, increases IB and IC. By KVL VC = VCC - IC RC, larger IC gives larger drop across RC, so VC falls. Positive in, negative out.
Emitter follower: 0° in-phase. VE = VB - VBE, VBE≈0.7V constant, so emitter follows base synchronously with same polarity and near-unity gain. Observed on dual-trace oscilloscope as inverted trace for CE and same polarity for CC.

questions.question: Derive the Miller Effect equation for an inverting amplifier stage and explain why it severely curtails the high-frequency response of Common-Emitter amplifiers.
questions.answer: Consider feedback impedance Zf between input (vin) and output (vout=-Av vin) of inverting stage. Current through feedback: if = (vin - vout)/Zf = vin(1+Av)/Zf. Input admittance seen: Yin = if/vin = (1+Av)/Zf. For capacitor Cf=Cμ=Cbc, Zf=1/(jωCμ), so Yin = jωCμ(1+Av) = jωCin(Miller), giving Cin(Miller)=Cμ(1+Av). For CE with Av=85 and Cμ≈8pF, Cin(Miller)=8pF*86=688pF. This capacitance appears in parallel with base-emitter capacitance and source resistance, forming low-pass filter that causes gain to fall rapidly above 450kHz. This limitation led to cascode configuration to eliminate Miller multiplication.

learnings: Distinction between DC equivalent circuit for bias point and AC small-signal model for gain and frequency response, and how superposition applies in amplifier analysis.
Use of bypass capacitor to increase AC gain without affecting DC bias stability, a standard technique in analog design.
Oscilloscope techniques: AC vs DC coupling, 10X probe to reduce capacitive loading, common grounding to avoid hum, and proper triggering for stable display of small signals.

Impedance matching concepts: CE provides voltage gain with medium input/output impedance, while CC provides near-unity gain with high input and low output impedance suitable as buffer stage in multistage amplifiers.
